children: Rajesh Baheti, Managing Director at Crosseas Capital Services, has renewed his push for the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) to keep derivatives expiry pricing away from the new closing auction session (CAS).

"As far as the derivatives market is concerned, keeping it away from purely CAS-determined prices is one of the things I have said from day one," he said, adding that only expiry-day futures and options contracts should settle using a volume-weighted average price (VWAP) calculated between 2:45 pm and 3:15 pm, while the rest of the market continues trading until 3:40 pm as usual.

Baheti's remarks come as SEBI reviews the closing auction mechanism after data showed sharp, unexplained price swings on expiry days — including a drop he said was "a 2,000-point drop in the Sensex, a 2,500-point drop in the BANKEX on the day of the monthly BSE expiry."

He also urged the regulator to penalise traders who place aggressive buy or sell orders near the close and then cancel or modify them, calling this a key driver of the volatility that has made expiry-day trading a lottery.
This is an edited transcript of the interview.
Q: Just first thoughts on the new pre-open session.
A:

I have held my view that I don't even have a problem with the closing auction session. The methodology per se does not bother me at all. It is the way the global markets have designed their methodology, and we are following it. There is no problem with either the closing auction session or the opening auction session, as proposed.

The issue was very clearly that till such time as the closing auction session got enough liquidity and depth, it was likely to create unnecessary volatility. And the problem was that settling the entire derivatives settlement price based on the closing auction price was too much of a risk for the Indian system.

I continue to maintain that these sessions themselves are not a problem. Just the fact that if you were to settle the entire derivatives market based on them, that would be a problem. As far as the opening auction is concerned, nothing settles based on that, so it's clearly not a problem.
Q: Does anything change for traders, etc., in the pre-open, at all? What should they be mindful of, Rajesh?
A:

Not really. If imbalances earlier also gave you the occasional odd freak trade up or down, they will continue to do so, but nothing gets decided based on that. It's not a settlement. Nothing settles based on that. So, you could choose to participate, look for some better prices, or you could then come in later. So, I don't think it is a negative for anybody, nor is the closing auction session, unless the derivatives settlement gets linked to it.
Q: So, nothing to celebrate or criticise, per se, in the new rule.
A:
Absolutely.

Q: I remember you talking about this every time you've been on, and we've done so many of these discussions and programs. So, I think it got to the regulator. The message, essentially, and the feedback, etc., and they've been holding consultations, to be fair, with a range of stakeholders. And exactly after a month of starting this new method, they're saying that they'll come up with something. Just your thoughts.
A:

So, no system is going to be perfect. Even the one that I have suggested, to delink the settlement, is not going to be perfect, but it's a temporary truce till such time as you see closing auctions getting that 10% or 15% of the daily volumes. If and when they do get it, and the prices remain close to where the mood of the market is, then sure, you can even merge the two.

But till such time as this closing auction gets the requisite depth and volumes, it would have been very dangerous to have the F&O settled based on those prices. And I think the regulator, having seen four weeks of data, has realised that something is amiss in terms of the way the settlement prices happen, especially in relation to expiry contracts and expiry days, and that those movements are not warranted in terms of the fundamentals of what has happened between 3:15 and 3:40. Therefore, those prices hurt some option sellers and create unnecessarily lottery-like situations for option buyers.
Q: There's a report that suggests that maybe a hybrid model is being proposed, mixing the old VWAP model as well as the CAS session. You know, what's your view on that?
A:

So, the problem I see with a hybrid model is that then the passives will come and say, "Look, we're not going to take care of tracking errors because if it's going to be 50% or 70% of the old style and 30% of the new style, sure enough, some volatility will be contained, but that doesn't solve the problem for which CAS was introduced in the first place."

As a derivatives trader, I really had not much problem with the half-an-hour weighted average, but there was some manipulation, for which SEBI had issued some orders. So, no system is going to be perfect.

I think if CAS and TWAP or VWAP, or some kind of weighted average, is taken between the two, it's going to go back to those passives, and they will come and complain that we're still getting those tracking errors.
So, I don't know what the number one solution is, but as far as the derivatives market is concerned, keeping it away from purely CAS-determined prices is one of the things I have said from day one.
Q: No system is going to be perfect. But if I were to ask you what, to your mind, is the best way to do it, what would you say?
A:

I have suggested a couple of things. One is to expire only the expiry-day contracts. So, not all the F&O contracts—only the expiry-day contracts should settle at 3:15. You can do a 2:45 to 3:15 VWAP, as was happening before, and the rest of the contracts can continue to trade till 3:40, as they continue to do, because they don't get influenced by the CAS anomalies.

The second thing is that what happens in CAS is that people unnecessarily enter very aggressive orders. Now, aggressive orders are those buy orders that come in above the closing price or the sell orders that come in below the closing price. Maybe SEBI should penalise modification and cancellation of aggressive orders so that once you put an aggressive order, it becomes very difficult to pull it out and then change the price again.
Q: You're saying that, at 3:00, for example, under the first suggestion, the expiry-day contracts are expired on VWAP, right?
A:
At 3:15. At 3:15 - only the expiry-day contracts. Yes.
Q: And then you continue with the cash market, of course, and the F&O market also, right? It goes on.
A:
Yes, because there are a bunch of contracts that don't expire, so there's no need to discontinue them at 3:15.
Q: And the rest of the F&O market continues to trade till 3:40, like it does now. There's no problem because there's no expiry after that.
A:
There's no expiry.
Q: And is this a big problem, the practice of putting in aggressive orders and then withdrawing them? Have you noticed that this is a big reason for these big swings?
A:
Absolutely. What was the reason? I can't explain anything else that created that 2,000-point drop in the Sensex and the 2,500-point drop in the BANKEX on the day of the monthly BSE expiry.

So there had to be some aggressive orders that were put in to take the index down 3%, and they were pulled out in that window, which allowed them to be pulled out. Now, clearly, something was amiss. There was no intention to trade those orders.

So aggressive orders are the ones that change the price, and if you want to trade, sure, you should be allowed to trade, but you shouldn't be allowed to show them, pull them out, or modify them at the last moment.

Q: And to that first point about expiring only the expiry-day contracts, assuming, say, between 2:45 and 3:15, is there any global precedent? Will this be widely accepted, or would there be some issues if this were to be implemented?
A:

No, when you expire a contract and what constitutes a settlement price is declared in advance, the market knows what it's going to settle at. The market only wants a fair price. It doesn't matter whether it's at 2:45 or 12:30.

We had currencies expiring at 12:30 pm in the middle of the trading day. So, there are enough global examples. The S&P triple-witching quarterly contracts expire based on the morning prices. They don't expire based on the closing prices at all.
So, once you set a time and people expect that the markets will trade continuously, they would get the kind of theta decay that is required or associated with a market that's so close to settlement.
What was not happening today was that the move between 3:15 and 3:40 was larger than the entire day's move. The entire expiry-day trade became a kind of lottery.

Q: We had the BSE MD & CEO with us the other day, and we were talking about how exchange volumes have suffered because of this. Not just BSE, but I guess overall. Do you think this change—for example, if they were to go with what you've suggested—will take care of some of that as well?
A:

There have been a lot of changes aimed at reducing volumes in the market, including the RBI circular on proprietary trading and the leverage that proprietary traders can take. So that trajectory is already on its way down.

But this was creating an anomaly that made the risk go up. An unnecessary increase in risk will discourage trading. And you don't want to control trading by making it riskier to be in the market. You can use every other direct measure.

So, I don't think it was intended to have this effect. As I said earlier also, it is an unintended consequence. And clearly, the regulator is now seeing that there is some problem with the way the F&O settlement price is determined, and that the best way, as far as I'm concerned for now, is to expire the contracts before the CAS session comes in.
The CAS session was meant for the passives. I don't think the passives will have a problem because they don't participate in the F&O space.

title: SEBI should keep F&O expiry pricing out of closing auction: Rajesh Baheti
